claims.text: The anomalous stress–strain behavior of HfNbTaTiZr is primarily governed by atomic-scale clustering.
The anomalous thermoelastic behavior of HfNbTaTiZr is primarily governed by atomic-scale clustering.
Varying Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr with compensating Hf concentrations produces atomic-scale clustering.
Atomic-scale clusters produce local thermal-expansion mismatches.
Local thermal-expansion mismatches modulate dislocation mobility.
Local thermal-expansion mismatches modulate phase stability across temperature.
The as-cast nominally equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr baseline is homogeneous.
The equiatomic baseline has a uniform atomic distribution without pronounced clustering.
Short-range-order clusters act as dislocation-pinning centers.
Short-range-order clusters create sites of heterogeneous strain.
Cluster-induced thermal-expansion mismatch generates internal stress during thermal cycling.
At high temperature, cluster-associated internal stresses enhance dislocation pinning and thereby increase creep resistance.
At lower temperatures, atomic clusters modify the elastic moduli.
During plastic deformation, atomic clusters act as barriers and increase hardening.
Greater Hf-driven clustering will increase tensile-creep resistance at approximately 1250 °C relative to the equiatomic baseline.
Greater Hf-driven clustering will alter elastic-modulus trends over 293–1100 K relative to the equiatomic baseline.
Greater Hf-driven clustering will increase hardening after simulated aging at 600–800 °C relative to the equiatomic baseline.
The proposed clustering mechanism unifies the reported creep, cold-rolling, elastic-modulus, and aging-hardening observations.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes the unresolved behavior of HfNbTaTiZr primarily to clustering, but the stated equiatomic material whose earlier behavior is to be explained is defined as homogeneous and lacking pronounced clustering. The hypothesis does not explain how clustering governs that baseline behavior if clustering only increases after compositional modification.

The conditions associate creep with approximately 1250 °C and 600–800 °C with aging, whereas the boundary describes approximately 600–1250 °C as the creep range, inconsistently reassigning the aging temperatures to creep.
